extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars and practitioners of Indian classical arts and general readers interested in Indian aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply the classical Indian theory of rasa as described in texts like the Natyashastra and Abhinavagupta, including the taxonomy of rasas, bhavas, and the means by which rasa is produced in performance, poetry, music and visual arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goal of art: produce rasa / transport audience
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the Rasa theory of the Natyashastra, entertainment is a desired effect of performance arts but not the primary goal. Instead, the primary goal is to transport the audience into another, parallel reality full of wonder and bliss, where they experience the essence of their consciousness and reflect on spiritual and moral questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aims of art include producing repose and relief for the distressed, but the essential evaluative standard is the creation of rasa that lifts and transports spectators toward expression of ultimate reality and transcendent values. Entertainment, reviews or awards are not the sole measures of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa sutra: determinants, consequents, transitory states
rubrics_metrics.description: “Rasa is produced from a combination of Determinants (vibhava), Consequents (anubhava) and Transitory States (vyabhicaribhava).” — Natyashastra 6.109
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any analysis or creation aiming to produce rasa must consider the interplay of vibhavas (causes/contexts), anubhavas (expressions/effects) and vyabhicaribhavas (transitory or ancillary emotions). This formula is central to how rasa arises in a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vibhavas: alambana and uddipana (determinants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vibhavas means Karana or cause: it is of two kinds - Alambana, the personal or human object and substratum, and Uddipana, the excitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting scenes or poetic situations, clearly establish the alambana (the central person/object that grounds the emotion) and the uddipana (stimuli that intensify the emotion) to generate the intended rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhava categories and Sthayibhavas mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the Natyashastra, bhavas are of three types: sthayi (stable), sanchari (travelling/ transitory) and sattvika (pure). The Natyashastra lists eight Sthayibhavas with eight corresponding rasas: Rati (Love), Hasya (Mirth), Soka (Sorrow), Krodha (Anger), Utsaha (Energy), Bhaya (Terror), Jugupsa (Disgust), Vismaya (Astonishment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective creation of rasa relies on developing a stable sthayibhava that will be sustained and enriched by sanchari and sattvika bhavas. Map intended rasas to their sthayibhava foundations when composing or performing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sattvika bhavas (physiological/emotive effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Natyashastra outlines eight anubhavas or sattvika bhavas: Stambha (Stupefaction), Sveda (Sweating), Romancha (Feeling thrilled), Svarabheda (Break in voice), Vepathu (Trembling), Vaivaranya (Pallor), Ashru (Tears), Pralaya (Swoon or death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sattvika bhavas are spontaneous psychophysical signs of intense emotion; their authentic depiction by performers (or evocation in text) strengthens the authenticity of the rasa experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of primary rasas (original eight, later nine) with attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata Muni enunciated eight rasas: Śṛṅgāra (Romance/Love), Hāsyam (Laughter/Comedy), Raudram (Fury), Kāruṇyam (Compassion), Bībhatsam (Disgust), Bhayānakam (Horror/Terror), Vīram (Heroism), Adbhutam (Wonder/Amazement). Later authors added a ninth rasa, Śāntam (Peace/Tranquility). Each rasa traditionally has a presiding deity and a specific colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for a particular rasa, creators can use the canonical names, emotional definitions, and associated ritual/visual markers (deity, colour) as heuristic guides. Note that rasas may have sub-categories (e.g., śṛṅgāra includes erotic sringara and devotional bhakti).

rubrics_metrics.name: Śāntam rasa: unique role and integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Later authors added a ninth rasa, Śāntam: Peace or tranquility. Śāntam functions as an equal member of the set of rasas but is distinct as the most clear form of aesthetic bliss; Abhinavagupta likens it to the string of a jeweled necklace that gives form to the other rasas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Śāntam’s acceptance was historically contested; its role is both integrative (gives form to other rasas) and elevated (approximates spiritual bliss). Use it deliberately when aiming for contemplative or transcendental aesthetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abhinavagupta’s measure of artistic success
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Abhinavagupta, the success of an artistic performance is measured not by the reviews, awards or recognition the production receives, but only when it is performed with skilled precision, devoted faith and pure concentration, so that the artist gets the audience emotionally absorbed into the art and immerses the spectator with the pure joy of a rasa experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate performances by the degree of audience immersion and the artist’s technical and spiritual commitment; prioritize precision, devotion and concentration over external accolades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sahṛdaya: the aesthetic appreciator requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Abhinavagupta defines sahṛdaya as spectators who 'have been exposed to appreciation of literary work and who have made it a habit to think about the literary work'—they attune their minds to create the reflection of poetic emotions. Aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdayatā) is crucial and requires fullness of delight and receptivity, including from painful experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rasa theory assumes an audience with cultivated receptivity; creators should consider the sahṛdaya when aiming for subtle or complex rasas, and pedagogically cultivate audience sensitivity through exposure and contextual framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry effectiveness: content and form create rasa
rubrics_metrics.description: In Indian poetics, ancient scholars state that a literary composition's effectiveness depends on what is stated and how it is stated (words, grammar, rhythm), which creates its rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing poetry or lyric prose, attend to diction, syntax and prosody as inseparable from emotive effect; form (meter, rhythm) and semantic content jointly produce rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of creating rasa in performance: abhinaya (gesture and expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasas are created through various means, and the ancient Indian texts discuss many such means. For example, one way is through the actors' gestures and facial expressions. Expressing Rasa in classical Indian dance form is referred to as Rasa-abhinaya.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers should cultivate a codified repertoire of gestures, facial expressions and bodily techniques (abhinaya) to reliably evoke the intended rasa in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa in music: raga as mood-specific creation
rubrics_metrics.description: In Indian classical music, each raga is an inspired creation for a specific mood, where the musician or ensemble creates the rasa in the listener. Predominantly, ragas and musical performances in Hindu traditions aim at rasas producing love, compassion, peace, heroism, comic or wonder feelings in the listener.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical composition and performance should align melodic, rhythmic and timbral choices to the target rasa; consider traditional mappings between ragas and emotional flavors and their sub-categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa in visual arts and architecture: drives form and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: In the theories on sculpture and architecture (Shilpa Shastras), the rasa theories, in part, drive the forms, shapes, arrangements and expressions of images and structures. Some Indian texts on sculpture suggest nine rasas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers and sculptors should select formal features (posture, facial expression, composition, ornamentation, spatial arrangement) that embody and elicit the intended rasa. Use canonical rasa associations (including colours and iconography) as compositional tools.
